title: Respond correctly to control defensive behaviour in animals

lessons.title: Possible responses to defensive behaviour
lessons.html:
When an animal defends itself

Defensive behaviour is an animal's way of saying "I feel threatened". A cow protecting her calf, a ram butting, a horse kicking or a sow charging are all defending themselves. How you respond decides whether the situation calms down or someone gets hurt.

Possible responses

SituationCorrect responseWrong response
Cow with calf faces you, head downStop, back away slowly, do not come between cow and calf, give her spaceRunning towards the calf, shouting
Bull paws the ground in the campKeep facing him, move calmly to the nearest fence or vehicle, leave the campTurning your back and running in open veld
Ram backs up to buttStep to the side, keep a hurdle or gate between youBending down in front of him
Horse lays ears back and turns hindquartersMove out of kicking range, speak calmly, approach later from the shoulderStanding directly behind it
Sow barks at you near pigletsLeave the pen, use a pig board when you returnPicking up a squealing piglet in front of her
Animal panics in the crushStay out of reach, keep quiet, let it settle before continuingHitting it or putting your arm through the bars

The general rules

  1. Stop what is causing the stress if you can: noise, a dog, a person too close.
  2. Increase the distance: step back out of the flight zone.
  3. Stay calm and quiet: animals react to your fear and noise.
  4. Get to safety: use your escape route, a gate, fence or vehicle.
  5. Tell your supervisor and plan a safer way to finish the job.

Under supervision you will practise these responses, for example moving a cow and calf through a gate or working sheep with a ram in the pen.

lessons.title: Observing and reporting behaviour
lessons.html:
Watching carefully

Good stockmen watch animals all the time. Small changes can warn you before an animal becomes dangerous or shows that it is sick.

What to observe

  • Body position: head low, side-on, back arched, leg raised.
  • Ears and eyes: ears pinned back, white of the eye showing, staring.
  • Sounds: bellowing, snorting, grunting, barking (pigs), stamping.
  • Movement: pawing, pacing, circling, charging, refusing to move.
  • Group behaviour: animals bunching tightly, one animal alone, fighting.
  • Triggers: what happened just before: a dog, a stranger, a noisy vehicle, a new calf, a sick animal.

Reporting

Tell your supervisor the same day about any animal that shows aggressive or defensive behaviour. Say:

  • Which animal (tag number, ear mark, colour, camp).
  • What it did.
  • When and where.
  • What you think caused it.
  • Whether anyone was hurt.

Some farms keep a record book or tag dangerous animals. A bull that charged once is likely to do it again; everyone must know. Some animals may need to be culled because they are too dangerous to keep.

Example report

"Tuesday morning in camp 4, cow with orange tag 217 charged me when I came close to her new calf at the water trough. I moved behind the trough and left the camp. Nobody was hurt. The calf looks healthy."

Showing what you saw

If you find it hard to explain in words, you can show your supervisor the animal, draw a simple picture of how it stood, or show the position with your own body. The aim is that the team understands the danger.

lessons.title: Correct reactions and procedures
lessons.html:
Reactions that reduce risk

  • Move slowly and speak calmly so animals always know where you are.
  • Never get between a mother and her young.
  • Never turn your back on a bull, boar, ram or stallion.
  • Do not stand directly behind horses, cattle or donkeys.
  • Do not enter a pen or crush with an animal unless the job needs it and someone is with you.
  • If an animal charges, get behind a solid object or over a fence. Do not try to outrun it in the open if there is cover nearby.
  • If you are knocked down, curl up and protect your head, and roll away towards cover when you can.

Correct working procedures

  1. Plan the job: which animals, which pens, how many people, what equipment.
  2. Check facilities: gates, races and crush in good order, no broken rails or slippery floors.
  3. Wear PPE: safety boots, overalls, gloves where needed.
  4. Work in pairs with large or dangerous animals. Tell someone where you are.
  5. Know your escape route before entering any pen or camp.
  6. Use handling aids: flags, paddles, pig boards, halters. Never use sticks to hit, electric prodders only as farm policy allows and never on the face or sensitive areas.
  7. Keep dogs under control.
  8. Handle animals quietly and in groups; avoid isolating one animal.
  9. Stop if things go wrong: let animals settle, re-plan, ask for help.
  10. Report injuries, near misses and dangerous animals.

Treating animals cruelly is against the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962. Calm, kind handling is also safer and gives better production: stressed animals grow more slowly and give less milk.

Key points

  • When an animal is defensive: stop, step back, stay calm, get to safety, report.
  • Observe body position, ears, eyes, sounds and triggers.
  • Report which animal, what, when, where and why.
  • Never get between a mother and young or turn your back on a male.
  • Plan, work in pairs, use handling aids and know your escape route.

quiz.question: A cow with a new calf faces you with her head down. What should you do?

options.text: Stop, back away slowly and give her space

quiz.question: A bull paws the ground in an open camp. What is the correct reaction?

options.text: Turn your back and run across the veld
Keep facing him and move calmly to a fence or vehicle

quiz.question: What should a report about a defensive animal include?

options.text: Which animal, what it did, when, where and the likely cause

quiz.question: Why is a bull that charged once a continuing danger?

options.text: He is likely to do it again
